In this setting, given an $n$-vertex graph, the goal is to decide in time $n^{O(1)}2^{o(k)}$ if a solution of size at most $k$ exists. Inspired by recent results in kernelization for structural parameters, we investigate subexponential algorithms for the Vertex Cover (VC) problem, but parameterized by distance-to-triviality instead of solution size. More formally, given a fixed "trivial" graph class $\mathcal{C}$, the problem takes as input $(G,X,k)$, where $G \setminus X \in \mathcal{C}$, and asks if $G$ admits a vertex cover of size at most $k$. Our goal is to design algorithms for this problem running in time $n^{O(1)}2^{o(|X|)}$. The motivation is that, since $|X|$ is typically arbitrarily smaller than $k$, such algorithms might be faster than ETH-tight subexponential algorithms parameterized by $k$. We identify two sets of sufficient conditions under which the problem admits a subexponential algorithm: one for the case where $\mathcal{C}$ is the class of paths, and another for the case where $\mathcal{C}$ is the class of graphs of constant treedepth. We also provide two applications of these algorithmic results: we prove that $s$-string graphs and pseudo-disk graphs satisfy the first set of conditions, whereas string graphs satisfy the second set. The two sets share a common condition that might be of independent interest, as it implies a property that bounds the treewidth of any string graph in terms of a given modulator to a fixed graph class $\mathcal{C}$. Finally, concerning more restricted graph classes having the $ASQGM(ω)$ property (such as map graphs and $H$-minor free graphs), we prove a dichotomy, depending on the maximum treewidth in $\mathcal{C}$.

items.title: Finite-Step Algorithms for Input-Constrained Control Barrier Function-Based Safety Filters
items.summary: Control barrier function (CBF) safety filters commonly rely on quadratic programs (QPs) to modify nominal control inputs while satisfying safety constraints. For safety-critical applications, however, the solution must be computed reliably under actuator limitations and with predictable computational effort. General-purpose QP solvers typically rely on numerical convergence criteria, which do not directly provide finite bounds on algorithmic steps or distinguish solver failure from mathematical infeasibility. This paper considers CBF-QPs with a single affine safety constraint, componentwise input bounds, and diagonal quadratic weights. Exploiting the established scalar dual structure of continuous quadratic knapsack problems, we obtain a necessary and sufficient pointwise feasibility condition and an exact breakpoint-based solution procedure. The algorithm requires at most 2n positive breakpoint events for n inputs, reducing to at most n events when the nominal input is admissible. In the latter case, an exact saturation--redistribution algorithm computes the optimal solution in at most n passes. We further describe how the structured solution can be combined with verified floating-point constraint evaluation to distinguish certified feasible commands, certified infeasibility, and unresolved numerical cases. The resulting framework provides an exact and computationally predictable solution procedure for a practically relevant class of input-constrained CBF safety filters.

items.title: A Deterministic Algorithm for Eigenvalue Separation in Tridiagonal Matrices
items.summary: We develop a deterministic algorithm for separating the eigenvalues of Hermitian tridiagonal matrices by small diagonal perturbations. For $\|T\|_2\leq1$, $0<δ<1/2$, and $X=\mathrm{diag}(1,\ldots,n)$, our algorithm selects $t\in[0,δ/n]$ such that $D=tX$ satisfies $\|D\|_2\leqδ$ and $\mathrm{gap}(T+D)>c\,δ^2n^{-12}$ for an absolute constant $c>0$. The construction uses a classical convex weighted eigenvalue sum and its finite-scale slope variation. A tridiagonal localization argument turns near-degenerate eigenvalues into separated responses to the fixed diagonal direction, yielding a quantitative gap certificate. An adaptive interval selector then identifies a certifying window in at most $\lceil\log_2(16n^3)\rceil$ refinements, using $O(\log n)$ evaluations of the weighted eigenvalue sum to inverse-polynomial accuracy. A structure-exploiting implementation uses rigorous Sturm eigenvalue enclosures and adaptive precision to certify the stopping condition on six families of test matrices. The directly certified gaps are substantially larger than the worst-case analytical bounds, illustrating both the effectiveness of the construction and the conservatism of the universal certificate. Our results give a deterministic answer to the eigenvalue-separation question underlying the deterministic Minami perturbation problem for tridiagonal matrices.

items.title: Fast HOSVD via Randomized Preconditioning and Mixed Precision
items.summary: Computing dominant mode subspaces is a major cost in the higher-order singular value decomposition (HOSVD) and its sequentially truncated variant (STHOSVD). Randomized Tucker algorithms can reduce this cost by approximating the required subspaces from small sketches, but may introduce additional approximation errors. We exploit the extreme aspect ratios of tensor unfoldings, whose mode dimensions can remain manageable while being orders of magnitude smaller than the products of the remaining dimensions. Instead of directly approximating the desired subspaces, we sketch the entire unfolding at a scale comparable to its mode dimension to preserve its full row-space geometry, and use randomized preconditioning to recover the desired singular subspaces through small matrix factorizations. We develop randomized preconditioned HOSVD and STHOSVD algorithms incorporating numerical truncation, and further accelerate their large matrix multiplications using mixed precision. Our analysis shows that truncation adds only a term quadratic in the numerical threshold to the classical HOSVD tail-energy bound, while mixed precision introduces a relative \(O(\sqrt{u_\ell})\) correction to the tail-energy term and an additive \(O(u_\ell)\) term under suitable conditions, where \(u_\ell\) is the lower-precision unit roundoff. On synthetic and real tensors, our methods achieve speedups of a fewfold to several dozenfold over classical HOSVD and STHOSVD, with runtimes competitive with those of other randomized methods. The double-precision versions match the classical reconstruction errors to numerical precision, and the mixed-precision variants yield nearly identical errors.

items.title: Nonlinear Joint State and Noise Estimation under Packet Dropouts and Additive Measurement Corruption
items.summary: This paper investigates joint state and noise covariance estimation for nonlinear systems subject to dual reliability impairments: random packet dropouts and additive measurement corruption. This scenario poses challenging nonconjugate inference, as clean and corrupted measurements share an unknown baseline covariance $\boldsymbol{R}_k$ with fixed known corruption covariance $\boldsymbol{E}_k$. Packet reception is observable, whereas the authenticity of received measurements remains latent and must be inferred. To resolve this intractable estimation problem, we cast joint posterior inference as a variational optimization problem and develop a conjugate variational inference adaptive Kalman filter with dual reliability (CVIAKF-DR). The proposed method retains analytical updates for the prediction covariance and two reliability probabilities, while adopting CVI to estimate the state and baseline measurement covariance. The covariance update combines the analytical contribution from clean measurements with Monte Carlo gradient estimates for corrupted measurements. Numerical results on a re-entry tracking benchmark demonstrate the superior accuracy of the proposed method in both state and noise covariance estimation. Remarkably, even built upon the linear Kalman filtering (KF) framework that is originally designed for linear systems, our method achieves more accurate estimation performance than dedicated nonlinear filtering algorithms based on the cubature Kalman filter (CKF).

items.title: Learning Morse Lyapunov functions through invertible neural networks
items.summary: Towards data-driven stability certificates of dynamical systems, we are witnessing renewed interest in studying and exploiting the structure of Lyapunov functions. Especially Lyapunov functions that are locally quadratic (i.e., Morse) gained popularity ever since it was understood that they can be written as the norm squared of a diffeomorphism. This topological representation alludes to parametrizations using invertible neural networks. In this note we discuss when and how such functions can be learned. In particular, using neural ODEs (NODEs), we characterize Sobolev approximation of these diffeomorphisms on compact sets and show how this naturally relates to stability. We also connect our results to PLNets and supply numerical experiments for illustration.

items.title: The Exact Optimal Delivery Scheme for the Cyclically $L$-Separated Placement in Multi-Access Coded Caching
items.summary: This paper investigates the $(K, L, M, N)$ multi-access coded caching (MACC) system introduced by Hachem et al. The system consists of a server storing $N$ equal-sized files, $K$ cache nodes, each with a storage capacity of $M$ files, and $K$ users, each accessing $L$ consecutive cache nodes in a cyclic wrap-around topology. The server transmits coded information to the users via an error-free capacitated broadcast channel, such that each user obtains its own requested file as a combination of the server transmission and the accessible caches' content. Our objective is to minimize the worst-case transmission load over all possible user demands. First, for the cyclically $L$-separated placement, we derive a new converse bound using the acyclic index coding bound. By carefully counting all valid cache supports, the proposed converse improves upon an existing bound for the same placement. We then develop a linear coded caching scheme based on a novel determinant-based interference alignment strategy, which achieves the new converse bound exactly. Exploiting the determinant structure of a random generating matrix (each of whose columns corresponds to one user), this scheme simultaneously aligns interference across all users into low-dimensional subspaces, while preserving the decodability of their desired packets. Furthermore, by averaging acyclic index coding bounds over cyclic user permutations, we derive a general converse bound applicable to arbitrary uncoded cache placements. By combining the proposed scheme with memory sharing, we demonstrate that the achievable transmission load is within a factor of two of the global bound under uncoded placement. Finally, theoretical and numerical comparisons demonstrate that the proposed scheme generally achieves a strictly lower load than existing schemes.

items.title: Optimal Quadrature and the Curse of Dimensionality for a Veronese Class
items.summary: We study integration on a $3^d$-dimensional trigonometric space whose unit ball has all coordinate mixed partial derivatives bounded by one. With evaluations anywhere in $\mathbb{R}^d$, we determine the exact minimal worst-case error among all deterministic algorithms using at most $n$ function values. An optimal quadrature formula is obtained by truncating an exact product quadrature formula on $\{1/2, 1/2+π\}^d$. All weights are positive. For each error tolerance $0<\varepsilon<1$, the information complexity grows exponentially in $d$ with the common base $Λ\approx 1.10546546$. The correction of order $\sqrt{d}$ to the logarithm of the information complexity and the corresponding error limit are determined by the standard normal distribution function. For $b\ge 1$ and $n=\lceil b^d\rceil$, the error tends to one, one half, or zero according as $b<Λ$, $b=Λ$, or $b>Λ$.

items.title: CONGA: Compiling Gaussian Fiber Geometry for Structured Bayesian Inference
items.summary: In structured Bayesian models, a large latent block is often Gaussian conditional on a smaller set of parameters, yet generic inference methods relearn this geometry during warmup. We study how this structure can be used to construct transports for posterior inference. The conditional mean and precision determine exact affine maps, including symmetric Brenier and triangular Knothe-Rosenblatt maps, that separate a standard normal block from the remaining non-Gaussian core. KL and relative Fisher objectives then reduce to objectives on this core. We introduce CONGA, a compiler that identifies candidate Gaussian blocks and selects a temporal, spectral, or sparse implementation according to their structure and computational cost. Marginalization requires an identity established from the model; numerical evidence alone permits only a target-preserving change of variables, and a failed check leaves the model unchanged. On the Stock-Watson inflation model, CONGA improves minimum ESS per second by 12.5x for NUTS. It also restores convergence where the raw target fails: for WALNUTS on the same model, and for NUTS on a 6760-dimensional electricity load model reduced to 34 core coordinates. Experiments on graph-indexed fields show how coloring and fill affect the choice of map, including cases where retaining the original target is preferable. Code at https://github.com/vicgalle/conga

items.title: A Rollout-Based Approach to Real-Time Topology and Dispatch Control in the AI4RealNet L2RPN Benchmark
items.summary: Operating transmission networks under uncertain outages requires coordinating discrete network topology actions with continuous adjustments to generation and storage, while respecting operational constraints and real-time computational limits. We present a rollout-based controller that combines discrete and continuous decisions under the uncertain contingency policy of the L2RPN AI4RealNet 2026 challenge. Power-flow approximations and convex optimization identify the most promising actions, followed by short-horizon simulations to predict their effect on congestion, renewable curtailment, and redispatching costs. A further policy exploits the benchmark's specific attack protocol: keeping selected lines disconnected prevents some adversarial outages from being initiated. On the benchmark's $118$-bus network, the controller completed $189$ of $208$ final-test scenarios (score $64.39$) and achieved the second-best ratio of score to computation time among the five top-ranked entries, behind one that scored lower. Our results show that combining structured optimization with simulation-based action selection is effective even without a learned decision rule, and fast enough for real-time control. Code and reproduction material: https://github.com/DavidKrame/RAD_agent__AI4RealNet_competition.

items.title: Copying along Arithmetic Progressions Cannot Simulate Interleaving with Polylogarithmic Loss
items.summary: Two classical ways to compress a word are straight-line programs (SLPs), which build it by concatenating smaller pieces, and the Lempel-Ziv 77 (LZ77) factorisation, which copies earlier parts of it; their sizes are measures of repetitiveness. LZ77 approximates the smallest SLP efficiently: it has no more factors than a smallest SLP has size, and yields an SLP at most a logarithmic factor larger in near-linear time. Motivated by online prediction, Kosoy introduced zipline programs, which are analogous to SLPs but interleave their pieces round-robin instead of concatenating them. Her generalisation of LZ77, the arithmetic repetition system, describes a word by copies from one arithmetic progression of positions to a later one. Do arithmetic repetition systems approximate the smallest zipline program as well? Kosoy proved that the least size $\mathrm{ARC}(x)$ of an arithmetic repetition system for a word $x$ of length $n$ is at most a factor $O(n^{1/3})$ larger than the least size $\mathrm{ZLC}(x)$ of a zipline program for it, and asked whether this factor is tight. Her polynomial-time next-letter predictor makes $O(\mathrm{ARC}(x)\log n)$ mistakes, so a polylogarithmic factor would bound its mistakes by $\mathrm{ZLC}(x)\,\mathrm{polylog}(n)$, which no known polynomial-time predictor achieves. We show that the optimal exponent is $1/4$, not $1/3$: $\mathrm{ARC}(x) \le 2n^{1/4}\,\mathrm{ZLC}(x)$ for every word $x$, and at every large enough length $n$ some binary word has $\mathrm{ARC}(x) \ge n^{1/4-o(1)}\,\mathrm{ZLC}(x)$.

items.title: Branch-and-Cut for Maximum $k$-Independent Sets with Spectral Bounds
items.summary: We develop a branch-and-cut method for finding maximum distance-independent sets in graphs. Our approach solves a sequence of fixed-size clique problems, combining graph reductions with combinatorial and spectral bounds. We give a compact formulation, derive strengthened inequalities, establish conditions for using spectral information, and evaluate them in a comprehensive computational study.

items.title: A Convergence Analysis of the Random Feature Method for Linear PDEs
items.summary: The Random Feature Method (RFM) distinguishes itself among machine learning approaches to partial differential equations (PDEs) through its superior accuracy and computational efficiency. Nevertheless, the theoretical underpinnings of RFM remain incompletely elucidated. This paper provides a comprehensive analysis of RFM within the framework of kernel methods, focusing on two principal aspects: (i) approximation by finitely many random features in Sobolev norms and the PDE residual seminorm, and (ii) estimation over the induced reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) from finitely many noiseless collocation observations. We relate both problems to kernel ridge regression (KRR) and establish upper and lower bounds in terms of the eigenvalues of the associated integral operators under the respective assumptions. Combining the approximation and estimation lower bounds, we establish a lower bound under simultaneous restrictions on the numbers of random features and collocation observations. We further quantify how activation regularity affects these eigenvalues, obtaining algebraic upper bounds for finitely smooth activations and stretched-exponential upper bounds for analytic activations.

items.title: Convergence rates of moment--SOS hierarchies with correlative sparsity via gluing and projection
items.summary: This paper studies convergence rates of moment--SOS hierarchies with correlative sparsity. Following the method proposed in~\cite{tran}, we bound the Hausdorff distance between the set of sparse truncated moment sequences and sparse truncated pseudo-moment sequences. The central step is a quantitative gluing lemma on a clique tree: local moment errors and separator discrepancies in total variation control the error of a joint approximating measure. Over hypercube, polynomial kernels give the convergence rates $O((\log_2r)^3/r^2)$ for the correlative sparse quadratic module and $O(r^{-2})$ for the correlative sparse preordering, where the certificate degree is $2r$. On compact basic semialgebraic sets, slack variable lifting and global atom projection yield $O((\log_2r)^{3\Lo/2}/r^{\Lo})$ and $O(r^{-\Lo})$ with a Łojasiewicz exponent $0<\Lo \le1$. These bounds hold for fixed-degree Hausdorff distances and polynomial objective gaps. We also extend to result to the correlative sparse quadratic-module rate for scalar objectives with clique-local polynomial matrix constraints.

items.title: Advancing Cognitive Pairwise Comparisons for Human-Centric Artificial Intelligence and Data Science: A Human-in-the-Loop Framework
items.summary: Human-centric artificial intelligence and data science (HCAD) systems increasingly involve human-in-the-loop (HITL) interventions to overcome the limitations of fully automated machine learning algorithms, such as automation bias and the inability to incorporate tacit domain knowledge, and continuously improve predictive performance. Data transformations, feature selection, feature weighting, and model selection usually require laborious human involvement across iterations of artificial intelligence and data science (AI&DS) pipelines, making development a challenging and time-consuming process. The Cognitive Pairwise Comparison (CPC) framework is proposed as a human-centric methodology to elicit preferences and priorities in a structured format. To establish essential facets of human-centricity, this research advances the CPC methodology so that user preference elicitation can be systematically quantified in these challenging AI&DS tasks. To demonstrate the usability and validity of these facets, this study presents several applications within movie recommender systems using the MovieLens dataset. It exemplifies how the extended CPC framework can facilitate interactions between human judgments and data across supervised learning, dimensionality reduction, and unsupervised learning algorithms.

items.title: Analysis and Design of Spatially Coupled LDPC Codes for Pulsed-Jamming-Resilient Space Telemetry
items.summary: Jamming is a major threat to space telemetry downlinks, which operate under severe power and bandwidth constraints. This paper develops a jamming-aware analysis and design framework for protograph-based spatially coupled low-density parity-check (SC-LDPC) codes. For pulsed jamming with jamming state information (JSI) at the receiver, we derive a two-state protograph-based extrinsic information transfer (PEXIT) recursion that tracks the messages originating from clean and jammed symbols separately and merges them at the check nodes through a mutual-information-matched Gaussian approximation. For non-interleaved pulsed jamming, we map each pulse realization, through the serialization of the lifted codeword, to a profile of jammed fractions over the variable-node types, and we prove that, under random lifting, this profile determines the local channel-state statistics. The resulting position-dependent thresholds are the objective of a constrained differential-evolution search over protographs, coupling memories, and edge spreadings. At different code rates, the designed ensembles are compared with the Consultative Committee for Space Data Systems (CCSDS) accumulate, repeat-by-4, and jagged accumulate (AR4JA) LDPC codes whose block length matches the SC-LDPC constraint length, with longer AR4JA codes whose block length is comparable with the size of the sliding window decoder, and with non-optimized SC-LDPC codes. Under pulsed jamming with random pulse positions and with JSI, the ensembles designed over random pulse realizations, decoded through sliding window decoding, reach a bit error rate of $10^{-4}$ at lower signal-to-noise ratios than all the benchmarks.

items.title: Quantitative approximation for Fourier neural operators in controlled ordinary differential equations
items.summary: Fourier neural operators (FNOs) avoid the curse of parametric complexity when approximating the solution operator of certain partial differential equations (PDEs). While recent studies primarily focus on PDEs, in this article we derive upper error bounds for approximating the solution operator of controlled ordinary differential equations (CODEs) $\dot{y}=f(y,u)$ using a FNO. Under a Carathéodory setting and suitable regularity assumptions, including a smallness condition, we prove that the size of the FNO grows at most algebraically in $1/\varepsilon$, namely like $\varepsilon^{-(1+d/(2(s-1)))}$ up to logarithmic factors for GELU networks, and is thus sub-quadratic for sufficiently smooth $f$, where $d=1+n_y+n_u$ and $s$ denotes the Sobolev regularity of $f$. Our proof is based on emulating the Picard iteration through the layers of the FNO while exploiting the differentiation formula of the discrete Fourier transform. This result contributes to the quantitative approximation theory of FNOs for physically motivated problems and provides a theoretical foundation for leveraging a FNO as efficient forward surrogate for the solution operator of CODEs, especially in inverse parameter estimation where repeated evaluations of the forward operator are needed.

items.title: Positive Regulation of an Axial Dispersion Tubular Reactor by Optimal Boundary Feedback Control
items.summary: The dynamics of the reactant in an isothermal axial dispersion tubular reactor is considered. Our goal consists in designing the inlet reactant concentration, under the form of a state feedback law, in order to modify the state behavior according to relevant process requirements, while keeping the positivity and stability properties of the uncontrolled dynamics. The designed control is also constrained to be positive to respect physical requirements. First, we state and analytically solve a parameterized optimal feedback design problem. Next, we address a positive observer-based feedback stabilization problem. The results are illustrated by means of numerical simulations.

items.title: Practical Semantic Communication for General-Purpose Networks: Compression of High-Dimensional Embeddings Under Quantization
items.summary: This paper introduces a practical framework for semantic communication over wireless channels, focusing on the compression of high-dimensional embeddings under quantization and channel errors. Building upon a relaxed Gaussian Information Bottleneck (GIB) model, the approach provides analytical solutions for task-relevant information preservation, even with non-Gaussian targets. The framework relaxes traditional Gaussian assumptions, enabling effective compression for discrete and complex data such as text embeddings. It derives closed-form gradients for optimizing the compression matrix and establishes bounds linking continuous representations to discrete, noisy system performance. Comprehensive experiments on text classification tasks demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms task-agnostic quantization-based compression methods, maintaining high semantic fidelity at low bit budgets per embedding. The approach offers a scalable, interpretable, and resource-efficient solution for deploying semantic communication in general-purpose networks.

items.title: Unconditionally Positive Nonstandard Finite Difference Schemes for $p$-Laplacian Reaction--Diffusion Equations
items.summary: We propose a conservative, semi-implicit nonstandard finite difference scheme for the reaction--diffusion equation $u_t=λ(|u_x|^{p-2}u_x)_x+f(u)$, $p>1$, where, as is customary, the $p$-Laplacian is regularized by a parameter $\eps>0$. The scheme combines a denominator function, a lagged diffusion coefficient, and a nonlocal treatment of the loss part of the reaction. For every time step and mesh size we prove that the scheme is well posed and positive, that it preserves an invariant region $[0,K]$ whenever the reaction admits one, and that it reproduces every constant equilibrium exactly. Without reaction, it conserves mass, satisfies a discrete maximum principle, and, for $1<p\le 2$, decreases a discrete energy. An example shows that the energy may increase for $p>2$. The truncation error is $O(k+h^2)$ at interior nodes. Numerical tests confirm first order in time and second order in space, and show that the scheme remains positive and bounded for step sizes at which the explicit method breaks down.

items.title: Maximum principle preserving approximation of scalar conservation equations with a fractional Laplacian
items.summary: In this paper, we propose a maximum principle preserving continuous finite element method for scalar conservation laws augmented with a fractional diffusion operator of order $s\in (0,1)$. Conservation laws with fractional diffusion operators arise in a variety of physical models involving anomalous transport and nonlocal regularization, including geophysical flows, plasma physics, and nonlinear acoustics. The fractional Laplacian is approximated using a sinc-quadrature representation, yielding a resolvent-based formulation compatible with continuous finite elements and explicit strong stability preserving Runge--Kutta time integration. A first-order monotone scheme is constructed using graph viscosity and is shown to satisfy a discrete maximum principle under an explicit CFL condition. A high-order extension is obtained via entropy-consistent corrections and convex limiting, achieving second-order accuracy while preserving the maximum principle, and hence positivity, as well as mass conservation in the periodic setting. Numerical experiments, including applications to the Surface Quasi-Geostrophic equation, confirm the second-order accuracy and the robustness of the proposed method on unstructured meshes.

items.title: Optimal Importance Sampling Densities for Estimating Several Expectations at Once
items.summary: Simulation studies often estimate several quantities from a single sample, and the best importance sampling density depends on how the errors on these quantities are combined. We characterise the optimal auxiliary density for a general error criterion. We show that it is the nominal density reweighted by a weighted length of the vector of estimated functions, where the weights are set by the error criterion, or by the curvature of the loss when the criterion comes from a loss on the errors. We also provide a lower bound on the best achievable error. The optimal density is explicit for smooth losses, including the usual losses on covariance matrices. We also derive allocation laws for the cells of a histogram and characterise the minimax density for the probabilities of several events. When there is no closed form, we show how to compute the optimal density numerically.

items.title: A conic optimization framework for shape-constrained functional regression analysis
items.summary: Standard regression methods do not always guarantee that the estimated model reflects prior knowledge about how predictors relate to the response, which motivates constrained regression. When the effects to be estimated are smooth nonlinear functions, a natural family of constraints is that of shape constraints, such as sign, monotonicity, or curvature, which encode qualitative properties that these functions are often expected to satisfy. While shape-constrained estimation of smooth functions is well established in classical regression with scalar covariates and response, its extension to functional regression, where the coefficients are themselves functions, remains largely unexplored. In this paper, we propose the functional shape-constrained conic P-spline estimator (FunSCOPE), a unified framework for shape-constrained functional linear regression that covers scalar-on-function, function-on-scalar, and function-on-function models, and in which any combination of the shapes above can be imposed on the functional regression coefficient. Building on a P-spline approach, the desired shapes are expressed as conditions on the scalar regression coefficients, which leads to an estimation problem formulated as a conic optimization problem. For univariate coefficients, as in scalar-on-function, function-on-scalar, and a particular case of the function-on-function regression, the concurrent case, these conditions are both necessary and sufficient, in contrast to existing approaches, which provide only sufficient conditions; for bivariate coefficients, as in general function-on-function models, they are neither necessary nor sufficient. Numerical experiments show that FunSCOPE outperforms competing methods in terms of estimation error and computational time.

items.title: Network-Native DNN Architecture Synthesis for Distributed Inference
items.summary: Distributed deep neural network (DNN) inference typically follows a model-first paradigm, in which a predefined DNN is partitioned and deployed over a physical network. On irregular communication-computation topologies, however, this approach can create transmission bottlenecks and leave distributed resources underutilized. This paper reverses this perspective and asks: given a physical network, what kind of DNN can it naturally support? To answer this question, we propose a network-native DNN architecture synthesis paradigm in which the physical network topology directly defines inter-node neural dependencies. Neural computation is allocated across nodes under communication, computation, storage, synchronization, and latency constraints. We establish structural properties of the synthesis problem and develop linear programming (LP)-based Architecture Synthesis (LPAS), an efficient topology-guided algorithm that produces a feasible architecture with a computable bound on suboptimality. Experiments on physical networks of different sizes show that LPAS achieves relative gaps below 0.6% to the LP-derived upper bound, with substantially lower runtime than direct mixed-integer LP optimization on larger networks. Under matched network deadlines, the network-native architectures activate more compute nodes and utilize a larger proportion of available model-storage capacity than the model-first baseline. After training, the network-native models achieve higher classification accuracy across all evaluated dataset-precision settings, with the average gain of up to 10.69%. This network-native design paradigm thus turns the physical network from a deployment constraint into an architecture design primitive.

items.title: High-order Crank-Nicolson method via diagonal Padé factorization
items.summary: We present a numerical method to solve the time-dependent Schrödinger equation at arbitrary order of accuracy in the time step, particularly well suited for tridiagonal Hamilton operators. The method is based on a factorization of the diagonal Padé approximants of the matrix exponential into products of linear factors, which preserves tridiagonal matrix structure at every time step and yields a propagator of order 2q in the time step at a cost of O(qN) operations. The propagator is exactly unitary by construction, and at lowest order q=1 it reduces to the standard Crank-Nicolson algorithm. We further extend the method to any Hamiltonian admitting a decomposition into a sum of tridiagonal or diagonal operators via high-order split-operator techniques (McLachlan, 2022), retaining O(qN) scaling at each time step. We also analytically show and numerically verify that the precision is dictated by the split-operator method. This covers a broad range of physically relevant cases, including higher-dimensional systems, higher-order spatial discretizations, and non-separable potentials.

items.title: Sign Primal-Dual Gradient Dynamics for Supply-Demand Coordination under Binary Human Feedback
items.summary: This paper addresses supply-demand coordination, in which a supplier sets prices to balance the demands of multiple buyers against limited resources. Existing studies typically solve the supply-demand coordination problem with a distributed algorithm called primal-dual gradient dynamics (PDGD), assuming that each buyer discloses the value of its own utility or marginal utility function. In contrast, we assume that each buyer discloses only binary information, namely whether it wants more or less of the current amount, and propose Sign PDGD. Sign PDGD is a PDGD algorithm in which the buyers' update depends only on the sign information. We analyze the convergence of Sign PDGD by interpreting it as a sliding mode control (SMC). For a quadratic cost and linear constraints, we show that under a gain condition, the primal and dual variables converge to the optimal solution. Numerical simulations on a toy resource-sharing problem confirm the two-phase behavior of SMC and show that the primal and dual variables approach the optimal solution.

items.title: Speed-Robust Scheduling for Total Completion Time
items.summary: We study two-stage speed-robust scheduling for minimizing total completion time. Jobs must be partitioned into $M$ bags before an adversary reveals the speeds of at most $M$ machines. Each bag is then assigned to one available machine, and the jobs on each machine may be processed in any order independent of the bags. We compare with an optimal schedule that knows the speeds in advance and assigns jobs individually. This model has been studied for makespan minimization. We initiate its study for total completion time, as suggested by Stein and Zhong (TALG 2020). For an unknown number of identical machines, we show that the optimal deterministic robustness factor is exactly~$13/12$, both for unit-size jobs and for arbitrary processing times. For infinitesimally small jobs, the factor lies between $31/30\approx1.0333$ and $28/27\approx1.0370$, well below the optimal makespan factor of about $1.2071$. General speeds make the problem strictly harder: no deterministic algorithm is better than $1.2669$-robust, already for infinitesimally small jobs. We give a $25/16$-robust algorithm for arbitrary processing times and improve the guarantee to $1681/1152\approx1.4592$ for infinitesimally small jobs. Our main tools are a layer decomposition that extends guarantees from unit-size jobs to arbitrary processing times when one assignment satisfies them for every prefix in non-increasing processing-time order, and a threshold analysis of the bag counts produced by greedy assignment rules.

items.title: A Lifted Hessian-Riemannian Gradient Flow for LQR Synthesis under Passivity Constraints
items.summary: The static state-feedback gain that renders a linear system passive at an external port and minimizes a linear quadratic regulator (LQR) cost cannot be computed by convex optimization, since the passivity certificate and the LQR cost are coupled bilinearly through the common gain. A previous indirect approach restricts the gain to a convex inner approximation of the passivity region, which is conservative and whose construction scales exponentially with the number of gain entries. This paper proposes a direct approach. The set of strictly passivating gains is the image of a convex lifted set of inverse storage matrices and transformed gains. We describe this set by a strict linear matrix inequality and an affine equality for every feedthrough matrix with positive semidefinite symmetric part, including feedthrough matrices with a singular symmetric part, and minimize the LQR cost over it by a gradient flow whose metric is the Hessian of a logarithmic barrier. For multi-input systems, this Hessian is singular along gain changes that preserve the storage function, and we complete the metric along these directions by the metric of the gain space. We prove that the flow exists for all times, that every gain along the flow is strictly passivating with an explicit storage function, and that the cost decreases monotonically while the gains remain in a compact set of stabilizing gains. Numerical examples show that the flow attains a lower cost than the indirect approach, that the completion is required for multi-input systems, and that the flow can converge to a local minimizer on nonconvex passivity regions.

items.title: An adaptive Gaussian splitting scheme for linear Fokker--Planck equations
items.summary: We develop an adaptive numerical method for linear Fokker--Planck equations on $\mathbb R^d$, based on approximating the evolving probability density by linear combinations of Gaussian functions (LCGs). The method applies to polynomial-type drift fields, without requiring a gradient-flow structure or a stationary distribution. It relies on an operator splitting that separates diffusion and affine drift, for which Gaussian functions can be propagated exactly, from higher-order transport, whose evolution is approximated adaptively by LCGs. Both the number of Gaussian components and their means and covariances are adjusted to meet the prescribed accuracy tolerances. The adaptivity is driven by computable error indicators involving polynomial moments of Gaussians that can be evaluated analytically. We provide a rigorous error analysis that relates the approximation error to the indicators driving adaptivity and illustrate the performance of the scheme in several test cases.

items.title: Improved Approximation for Weighted $k$-Set Packing via a Simple Two-Phase Approach
items.summary: Weighted $k$-set packing asks for a maximum-weight collection of pairwise disjoint sets, each of cardinality at most $k$. For every fixed $k\in\mathbb Z_{\geq1}$, we give a polynomial-time algorithm with approximation factor $\left(1- 1/{\sqrt3} \right)k+O(\log k) \approx 0.4226k + O(\log k)$, improving the previous best factor of $0.4621k + O(\sqrt{k})$ through a simple two-phase approach. In a first phase, our algorithm constructs a packing by processing random weight buckets of varying widths with an unweighted packing algorithm. We show that a small expected weight of this packing relative to the optimum forces a large expected total surplus in the optimum. Surplus quantifies the potential for improving a packing through star swaps. In the second phase, we solve and round a configuration LP to turn sufficiently large surplus into an increase in expected weight. Our procedure can easily be derandomized.

items.title: Scaled boundary finite elements for FFT-based computational micromechanics
items.summary: We introduce a matrix-free FFT-based solver for three-dimensional linear elastic homogenization problems discretized by the scaled boundary finite element method (SBFEM) on a voxel grid. Owing to its analytical solution in the radial direction, the SBFEM discretization is inherently softer than fully integrated voxel finite elements, whereas its displacement-based formulation remains symmetric, conforming, and supports arbitrary stiffness anisotropy. These properties make SBFEM an attractive candidate for porous and highly heterogeneous microstructures, where existing voxel-based FFT discretizations offer no generally reliable choice: Reduced-integration hexahedral elements, equivalently the rotated staggered grid discretization, may suffer from hourglass instabilities in the presence of voids, whereas fully integrated hexahedral elements are often too stiff. The proposed discretization uses hexahedral SBFEM cells on the full voxel mesh of a regular periodic grid, retaining the simplicity of a fixed-resolution voxel representation without requiring adaptive mesh coarsening. The main contribution is a preconditioner based on the homogeneous SBFEM stiffness operator. We show that this preconditioner may be applied locally in Fourier space and that the condition number of the preconditioned system is bounded by the material contrast, independently of the grid resolution. This result enables a fully matrix-free implementation of the SBFEM-discretized problem, without assembling or storing the global stiffness matrix. Numerical experiments on a short-fibre reinforced composite, a polyurethane foam and a sand-based binder jet microstructure demonstrate robust convergence and competitive accuracy compared with established voxel discretizations. In particular, SBFEM remains stable for porous microstructures, for which reduced-integration hexahedral elements become unstable.

items.title: Bayesian variable selection via collapsed importance-weighted variational inference over discrete model spaces
items.summary: Bayesian variable selection under spike-and-slab priors provides interpretable posterior inclusion probabilities for individual predictors, but exploring large discrete model spaces using conventional Markov chain Monte Carlo methods can be computationally challenging. We develop a collapsed importance-weighted variational framework for Gaussian linear regression. The framework analytically integrates out the remaining model parameters and directly approximates the posterior over binary inclusion indicators using a factorised Bernoulli distribution. To improve posterior inclusion probability estimation while retaining the computational simplicity of the factorised variational family, we replace the conventional evidence lower bound with a tighter variational Rényi importance-weighted lower bound. We establish a finite-sample upper bound on posterior inclusion probability approximation errors and show that, under suitable conditions, the optimised variational inclusion probabilities converge to their exact posterior counterparts as the number of importance samples increases and the Rényi parameter decreases appropriately. We further establish that analytical marginalisation tightens the variational objective and the corresponding inclusion probability error bound, while reducing importance-weight variance and improving the asymptotic efficiency of importance-sampling post-processing. To address the challenges of estimating gradients with respect to the variational parameters when the inclusion indicators are discrete, we leverage recent advances in variance-reduced score-function estimators, together with an annealing strategy to stabilise optimisation. Simulation experiments and empirical applications demonstrate improvements in posterior inclusion probability estimation relative to standard variational inference and two existing variational approaches.

items.title: UNIDE: Cross-PDE Learning for Noise-Robust Discovery of Governing Equations
items.summary: Governing partial differential equations (PDEs) provide compact and interpretable descriptions of physical systems. Classical methods, such as sparse and symbolic regression, fit a new equation to each observed field: what is learned on one system is not carried to the next, and observation noise corrupts the derivative features they rely on. This paper introduces UNIDE (Unified Identification of Differential Equations), a data-driven approach that learns across PDE families to identify governing equations from new noisy trajectories. It integrates three components: a self-supervised denoiser trained without clean targets, an encoder shared across PDE families that predicts which candidate terms are active, and weak-form least squares with residual-based pruning that estimates their coefficients. We demonstrate UNIDE on synthetic one-dimensional trajectories from six PDE families with known term structures, including the Burgers and Kuramoto--Sivashinsky equations. We train one model per noise level and systematically compare UNIDE with SINDy, WSINDy, and PySR. The results show that UNIDE recovers the exact set of governing terms more often than all three at every noise level from $1\%$ to $80\%$. At $80\%$ noise, where the noise standard deviation is $0.8$ times that of the field, it recovers the exact terms for $92\%$ of held-out trajectories, whereas the best baseline recovers about $1\%$. UNIDE is also efficient: because its neural components are reused rather than refit, it identifies each new trajectory in $0.45$ seconds, $2.7$ times faster than WSINDy and $51$ times faster than PySR. These results demonstrate the potential of learning across PDE families for efficient equation identification under substantial observation noise.

items.title: Explicit topology control in isogeometric topology optimization using persistent homology
items.summary: Explicitly controlling structural topology remains a major challenge in topology optimization. While many implicit methods regulate topology only indirectly, available explicit strategies often focus on two-dimensional hole control or extend to 3D without a unified treatment of tunnels and cavities. This study proposes a differentiable, persistent homology-based framework for explicit topology control in 2D and 3D isogeometric topology optimization. A NURBS-represented density field induces a single sublevel filtration whose persistence diagrams quantify the connected components, holes in 2D, and tunnels and cavities in 3D directly. To enforce prescribed bounds on topological feature counts, weighted topological objectives are applied in a staged manner that coordinates the different homology dimensions. Each redundant feature is removed either by cutting or by filling according to the region of its corresponding persistence pair, avoiding the excessive structural changes associated with filling alone. The topological inverse mapping yields analytical sensitivities with respect to the density control coefficients, so that the resulting objective is readily incorporated into gradient-based optimization and solved by the method of moving asymptotes. Numerical experiments on 2D and 3D benchmarks demonstrate explicit and reliable topology control while maintaining competitive mechanical performance and stable convergence.

items.title: When is Uniform Sampling Optimal? Coresets for Distributional Clustering
items.summary: Recent work [1] settled the optimal worst-case strong $\varepsilon$-coreset size for Euclidean $k$-means in unrestricted dimension at $\tildeΘ(\min\{k^{3/2}\varepsilon^{-2}, k\varepsilon^{-4}\})$, showing that the natural target $\tilde{O}(k\varepsilon^{-2})$ is unattainable in general. For mixtures of $k$ isotropic Gaussian components with balanced weights and bounded scale imbalance in dimension $d\ge\log k$, we show that uniform sampling yields strong $\varepsilon$-coresets of size $\tilde{O}(k\varepsilon^{-2})$, without cluster separation. This saves a factor of $\min\{\sqrt{k},\varepsilon^{-2}\}$ over the worst-case bound, up to logarithms. For population approximation by independent, equally weighted samples, the near-linear rate is optimal up to logarithmic factors over this class. More generally, for datasets generated from an isotropic Gaussian mixture $μ$ satisfying a mild cost-comparison assumption, uniform sampling yields strong $\varepsilon$-coresets of size $\tilde{O}((kζ_μ+π_{\min}^{-1})\varepsilon^{-2})$, where $π_{\min}$ is the minimum component weight and $ζ_μ$ measures scale imbalance. Our proof uses a base-shift cost decomposition: one query center per component describes the base costs, and graph spanners control the sparse corrections from points switching centers. For general mixtures under cost and tail assumptions, we obtain $\tilde{O}((kζ_μ+π_{\min}^{-1})\varepsilon^{-2}\min\{\sqrt{k},\varepsilon^{-2}\})$ samples. We also prove a matching $\tildeΩ(\min\{k^{3/2}\varepsilon^{-2},k\varepsilon^{-4}\})$ lower bound for population approximation by uniform sampling from anisotropic Gaussian mixtures, even with equal weights and a shared covariance matrix. [1] Junqiu Hu, Lingxiao Huang, Jian Li, and Baoduo Xu. Tight coreset bounds for $(k, z)$-clustering in Euclidean and doubling metrics, 2026. arXiv:2610.34373.

items.title: Two-Stage Staffing with Random Arrival Rate: A Simulation Optimization Approach
items.summary: In service systems, the arrival rate in the same time period and day of the week exhibits randomness, yet can be more accurately estimated or forecast right before that period, which motivates a two-stage staffing scheme with advance base staffing and pre-shift surge staffing. Existing approaches usually impose strong assumptions on the arrival process and service systems' operational logic and other further approximations (i.e., stylized models) to derive explicit staffing policies. This paper proposes a simulation optimization approach (SOA) for more general arrival processes and service systems by effectively addressing some intertwined challenges. By recasting the original formulation into computationally tractable structures and designing an efficient coordinate-search algorithm, it constructs a two-stage staffing lookup table offline, which allows managers to make real-time surge staffing decisions without any further simulation. Comprehensive numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed SOA has significantly better staffing performance and substantially broader applicability compared to existing approaches. Even under the stylized models, the cost savings delivered by our SOA compared with existing approaches range from the low tens to several tens of percent, depending on different problem parameters; the advantage further amplifies when the actual problem deviates from the stylized models. In a nurse-staffing case study grounded in real-world data, the proposed SOA delivers approximately 8% to 13% cost savings over a state-of-the-art benchmark.

items.title: Neural Operator Approximation for Yau--Yau Nonlinear Filtering: Stability, Approximation, and Fast Computation
items.summary: Since the introduction of the Kalman filter, nonlinear state estimation has become an important topic in areas such as aerospace engineering, sensor design, and target tracking. Within the optimal filtering framework described by the Duncan-Mortensen-Zakai (DMZ) equation, Yau-Yau filtering (YYF) employs an offline-online decomposition: the Fokker-Planck-Kolmogorov (FKE) equations, initialized by a prescribed set of basis functions, are solved offline, and the prior density is projected onto these basis functions during the online stage. However, this approach still faces two computational challenges: solving multiple FKEs offline can be computationally expensive, and the online projection becomes costly when filtering is performed repeatedly or in high-dimensional settings. To address these limitations, we develop a neural operator filter (NOF) that directly learns the mapping from the prior density to the posterior density, thereby eliminating both the expensive offline FKE solves and the online projection. The underlying operator is approximated using a Fourier neural operator (FNO). Numerical experiments on several challenging filtering systems verify both the effectiveness and accuracy of our method, and we further provide a rigorous theoretical analysis of its stability and approximation error.

items.title: Structure-Preserving Neural Time-Stepping for Gradient-Flow PDEs via Onsager's Variational Principle
items.summary: We propose a unified Onsager-based neural time-stepping (ONTS) framework for solving gradient-flow partial differential equations with conserved and nonconserved dynamics. Unlike conventional neural time-stepping methods that directly parameterize the evolving state, the proposed framework employs spatial neural networks to approximate the Onsager process variables, namely, the rates in nonconserved systems and the fluxes in conserved systems. Within this Eulerian framework, we develop three complementary schemes: an explicit least-squares scheme (E-ONTS), an implicit variational scheme (I-ONTS), and a predictor--corrector scheme (PC-ONTS) that combines explicit prediction with safeguarded implicit correction. For conserved systems, the flux-based formulation guarantees discrete mass conservation under periodic or no-flux boundary conditions. Furthermore, we rigorously establish unconditional discrete energy stability for the implicit schemes, provided that a suitable descent criterion is satisfied, without requiring global minimization of the neural variational objective. Numerical experiments for the heat, Allen--Cahn, Cahn--Hilliard, Fokker--Planck, and coupled Poisson--Nernst--Planck equations demonstrate the accuracy, robustness, and structure-preserving properties of the proposed framework.

items.title: A Staggered Discontinuous Galerkin Neural Network Method with a Computable Error Decomposition
items.summary: We develop a staggered discontinuous Galerkin neural network (SDGNN) method for scalar elliptic problems with a computable error decomposition. The staggered discontinuous Galerkin (SDG) method requires only local continuity of its trial functions and gives a square, inf-sup stable system without stabilization parameters; we carry this structure over to neural networks. Networks defined on the patches of a staggered mesh satisfy the SDG continuity conditions for all values of the network parameters, and the loss is the squared dual norm of the SDG weak residual. We show that the loss is equivalent, with computable constants, to the square of the training error, the distance between the SDG projection of the network and the SDG finite element approximation, so that the full error is bounded by the discretization error, a multiple of the square root of the loss, and the network projection error. The weak residual requires no derivatives of the networks, the boundary and convection terms carry no penalty or stabilization weights, and the scalar trial functions may jump across the midlines of the primal cells. Numerical experiments show that the square root of the loss tracks the error during the training, that prescribed jumps across a square and a circular interface are captured consistently over the initializations, and that the method is more accurate than physics-informed neural networks at the same parameter counts.

items.title: Hyperspectral imaging from diffractograms
items.summary: We consider an optical system with a periodic point spread function, such as a camera with a periodic diffractive filter array placed near the sensor. Such systems produce a monochrome image that we call ``diffractogram'', and that multiplexes the spatial and spectral information about the scene. We present a method to efficiently invert this forward model and recover the hyperspectral scene. The inverse problem is formulated as a large scale $\ell_1$-penalized least squares problem that is solved iteratively with the Alternating Direction Method of Multipliers (ADMM). A Krylov subspace solver, such as LSQR, may require tens to hundreds of iterations to approximatively solve the augmented least-squares problem required in each ADMM iteration. Here we present an exact direct solver for the augmented least-squares problems that exploits the periodicity of the point spread function. Each direct solve costs roughly as much as three LSQR iterations, eliminating inner iterations entirely. We validate the method on both synthetic and experimental datasets.

items.title: Degenerate Preconditioned Proximal Point Algorithms as Forward Methods for Nonmonotone Inclusions
items.summary: We study degenerate preconditioned proximal point algorithms (PPPA) for finding zeros of nonmonotone set-valued operators in Hilbert spaces under solution-relative $(U,V)$-semimonotonicity, with possibly indefinite $U$ and $V$. With a closed-range preconditioner $P$, the reduced PPPA dynamics admit a forward representation through the complementary resolvent of a parallel composition, without requiring monotonicity or admissibility. Relative semimonotonicity of the range-restricted operator transfers to the reduced forward map, allowing our forward theory for possibly set-valued mappings to yield Fejér estimates and residual rates. Under suitable conditions, including demiclosedness of the reduced map at zero, the projected PPPA iterates and shadows converge weakly to a common projected zero. Without demiclosedness, a counterexample shows that the projected sequences may converge to a point outside the projected zero set, even when the original operator is continuous. Bounded recovery condition yields weak convergence of the full (non-projected) shadows. The monotonicity modulus $U$ yields additional results: under suitable conditions, $U\succeqτP$ with $τ>0$ gives strong and linear convergence of the projected PPPA sequences, while $U\succeq-σP$ with $0\leσ<1/2$ still permits local linear rates under metric subregularity. These strong convergence and linear rate guarantees extend to the full shadows when a Lipschitz recovery estimate holds, such as when $U$ is strongly monotone on $\ker P$. For Chambolle--Pock and Douglas--Rachford splitting, we establish Lipschitz recovery even when $U=0$ by exploiting the primal--dual structure. Under suitable parameter conditions, full-shadow convergence guarantees, including $R$-linear rates, extend to the original PPPA iterates.

items.title: Optimal Dynamic Quantizers for Periodically Time-Varying Systems via Cyclic Reformulation
items.summary: This paper addresses the design of optimal dynamic quantizers for discrete-time linear periodically time-varying (LPTV) plants with discrete-valued inputs. Optimal dynamic quantizers, which minimize the worst-case output error caused by quantization, are well established for linear time-invariant (LTI) plants, whereas the corresponding design for plants with periodically time-varying dynamics has not been addressed. For square LPTV plants having relative degree one at every time phase, this paper derives an optimal periodic dynamic quantizer in closed form. The quantizer is constructed by applying the LTI theory to the cycled plant obtained by cyclic reformulation and reading off its periodic coefficient matrices block by block; its optimality is then verified directly, showing that it attains a performance lower bound determined by the largest instantaneous input-to-output gain over the time phases. The worst-case output error of general periodic dynamic quantizers is also characterized. The optimal quantizer is shown to be stable if and only if all invariant zeros of the cycled plant lie in the open unit disk, which is the condition that governs stable causal inversion of LPTV plants. A numerical example with comparisons to conventional quantizers illustrates the results.

items.title: A bound-preserving hybrid lattice Boltzmann method for scalar hyperbolic conservation laws
items.summary: Solutions to scalar hyperbolic conservation laws may develop discontinuities within finite time even from smooth initial data, while higher-order lattice Boltzmann (LB) methods tend to generate non-physical oscillations and out-of-bounds behavior near steep gradients. To address this issue, we first construct a first-order LB method with the upwind-type equilibrium distribution functions under the \(DdQ(2d+1)\) lattice structure, and establish its bound-preserving (BP) conditions. We then develop a second-order multiple-relaxation-time LB (MRT-LB) method by introducing the auxiliary source distribution functions, and analyze its \(L^2\) stability. Building on these, we propose a hybrid LB method that preserves the collision-streaming structure, by conservatively mixing first- and second-order updates through a convex constraint mechanism. We further establish the global BP (GBP), local BP (LBP), and relaxed LBP (RLBP) limiters in the hybrid LB method, together with the associated macroscopic BP constraints. Numerical experiments examine the convergence order, interface capturing performance, and discontinuity resolution capability of the proposed BP hybrid LB method. The results indicate that it effectively suppresses out-of-bounds behavior in the second-order LB method and reduces numerical dissipation in the first-order LB method, while maintaining the prescribed bounds and discrete mass conservation.

items.title: A proof of a conjecture on bipartite correspondence packing
items.summary: A correspondence cover assigns a set of possible colors to each vertex of a graph. For each edge, a matching between the two endpoint color sets specifies the forbidden color pairs. A correspondence coloring selects one color at each vertex so that no forbidden pair is selected. A full correspondence packing is a collection of such colorings that uses every color at each vertex exactly once. We prove a conjecture of Cambie, Cames van Batenburg, Davies, and Kang [Random Structures & Algorithms 64 (2024), 62--93]. For every sufficiently large $D$, there is a positive integer $k(D)=(1+o(1))D/\log D$ such that every correspondence cover of any finite bipartite graph has a full correspondence packing if each color has at most $D$ forbidden partners and each vertex has $k(D)$ colors. More precisely, we prove this conclusion with \[ k(D)=\left\lceil\frac{D}{\log D-2\log\log D-6}\right\rceil \] for every integer $D\ge\lceil e^{20}\rceil$.

items.title: Weighted Sum-Rate Optimization of Near-Field STAR-RIS-Aided ISAC Systems Under Hardware Impairments
items.summary: This paper investigates weighted sum-rate (WSR) optimization for a simultaneously transmitting and reflecting reconfigurable intelligent surface (STAR-RIS)-assisted multi-user multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) system operating under the energy splitting (ES) protocol. A hybrid propagation model is considered, where the base station (BS)-STAR-RIS channel follows far-field propagation, whereas the STAR-RIS-user channels are modeled using near-field spherical wavefronts. Practical hardware impairments (HWIs), including STAR-RIS phase perturbations and signal-dependent additive distortion at the BS and user equipment (UEs), are incorporated into the system model. Under this framework, the WSR maximization problem is formulated subject to radar beampattern, quality-of-service, transmit-power, and STAR-RIS ES constraints. The resulting problem is highly non-convex due to the coupling among the active beamformers, passive STAR-RIS coefficients, and HWI-dependent signal-to interference-plus-noise ratio expressions. An alternating optimization (AO)-based successive convex approximation framework is developed to iteratively solve the active and passive beamforming subproblems. Numerical results demonstrate stable convergence of the proposed algorithm and consistent WSR improvement over direct-link transmission. Besides, severe HWIs also lead to WSR saturation in the high transmit-power regime, whereas stringent sensing constraints reduce communication throughput. Increasing the STAR-RIS aperture and the number of BS antennas improves the achievable WSR, although the performance gain becomes limited under strong hardware distortion.

items.title: Parallelizable Interior-Point ADMM for Block-Structured Nonconvex Programs
items.summary: Physics simulation is an increasingly important computational primitive for AI, and local--global/ADMM splitting exposes its parallel structure but lacks matching finite-time convergence guarantees. We close this gap with two ADMM variants, Interior-Point ADMM (IP-ADMM), for block-structured nonconvex composite programs with smooth nonlinear inequality and affine constraints. A one-sided finite-activation wall keeps each constraint split state strictly feasible while the original-space infeasibility vanishes, giving closed-form constraint updates, one proximal call per objective block, and one equality-constrained quadratic consensus solve per iteration. \rev{To our knowledge, this makes IP-ADMM the first single-loop method that updates nonconvex inequality constraints locally and in parallel with finite-time convergence guarantees.} Ordinary IP-ADMM attains a CQ-free best-iterate weak-KKT rate of $O(K^{-1/3})$ or a banded Fritz--John rate of $O(K^{-1/4})$, which converts to KKT at $O(K^{-1/4})$ under a uniform constraint qualification; these are nearby-point certificates that reduce to conventional KKT for smooth blocks. A checkpoint variant, IP-ADMM-Ckpt, improves the asymptotic KKT exponent to $O(K^{-1/3})$. We also show how the bounds scale with the objective- and constraint-block counts and the coupling norm.

items.title: Rounded Potentials Certify Exact Maximum Flow
items.summary: The textbook certificate for maximum flow is lopsided: the cut takes one bit per vertex, while the flow takes one number per edge. Indeed, some graphs have $Θ(n^2)$ terminal pairs for which every maximum flow uses $Θ(n^2)$ edges. Yet we show that one short number per vertex suffices for both cut and flow: $n$ vertex potentials, each rounded to $O(\log(nW))$ bits, certify the exact maximum $st$-flow value in any directed graph with integer capacities at most $W$. Exact potentials can have exponentially large representations. Rounding them may violate flow conservation, but the total error across any cut is less than one unit, so integrality of cut capacities absorbs it. Checking conservation is local and linear in the capacities, allowing the same certificate to yield new bounds in four models (capacities are polynomially bounded unless stated otherwise): - Online annotated streaming. $\widetilde{O}(n)$ total cost (help plus space) for the maximum $st$-flow value, optimal up to logarithmic factors, answering a question of Thaler (ICALP 2016) on whether $o(n^2)$ is possible. - Broadcast proof-labeling. $O(\log(n+p))$-bit labels certifying a maximum $st$-flow value of $p$ in directed and undirected graphs with arbitrary capacities, optimal for $p\ge n^{Ω(1)}$, settling that regime of a question of Korman, Kutten, and Peleg (Distributed Computing 2010). - Merlin-Arthur verification. $\widetilde{O}(n^3)$ time and $O(n^3\log n)$ proof length for directed All-Pairs Max-Flow, improving on previous verification times of $n^{4+o(1)}$ for general capacities and $n^{3.5+o(1)}$ for unit capacities, and answering a question of Akmal (TheoretiCS 2024). - Nondeterministic algorithms. $O(n^{3.614})$ time for directed All-Pairs Max-Flow, or $n^{3.5+o(1)}$ if $ω=2$: the first subquartic bound for general edge capacities, answering a question of Trabelsi (SODA 2025).

items.title: Online and Fully-Dynamic Sorting
items.summary: Online sorting asks how to place $n$ sequentially arriving elements in an array to minimize the sum of absolute differences between consecutive elements. Fully-dynamic sorting further extends the problem to allow both element insertions and deletions. Without recourse, these problems face strong lower bounds on the competitive ratio: $Ω(\sqrt{n})$ for online sorting and $Ω(n)$ for fully-dynamic sorting. In sharp contrast, we show that allowing only poly-logarithmic recourse yields at least exponential improvements in the competitive ratio for both problems:(1) Our main algorithmic result is a deterministic fully-dynamic sorting algorithm that is $O(\log^2 n)$-competitive and has $O(\log^4 n)$ amortized recourse per update. We complement this with a lower bound showing that any deterministic algorithm with any $O(\mathrm{polylog}(n))$ competitive ratio has amortized recourse at least $Ω(\sqrt{\log n})$.(2) For the insertion-only setting, we establish a family of approximation--recourse tradeoffs, including $O(\log\log n)$ competitive ratio with $O(\log\log n)$ amortized recourse. Given the lower bound in the fully-dynamic case, this result shows that the insertion-only problem yields exponentially better bounds than the fully-dynamic one.(3) Finally, we show that the stronger approximation-recourse tradeoff for the insertion-only case extends to the fully-dynamic setting when the array has $(1+\varepsilon)n$ space.

items.title: Hyperbolic Polynomial Certificates: Universality, Cubic Exactness, and a Weak--Strong Separation
items.summary: We study certificates of polynomial nonnegativity based on hyperbolic polynomials and their parameterized Bézoutians and establish three results. First, in the unrestricted hyperzout model of Ng and Saunderson, every nonnegative real form of degree $2r$ in $m$ variables admits a hyperzout representation using an auxiliary hyperbolic form of degree $2r$ in $m+1$ variables with parameters $k=1$ and $μ=r+1$. Second, every homogeneous hyperbolic cubic in five real variables is SOS-hyperbolic in Saunderson's fixed-direction sense: for each hyperbolicity direction $e$, $B_{p,e,v}$ is a matrix SOS for every $v\in\Lam(p,e)$. Third, a general localization proposition turns an interior-SOS central Wronskian and a non-matrix-SOS central Bézoutian into a two-direction weak--strong separation. An icosahedral seed gives a rational example of degree $46$ in $43$ variables for which every $W_{u,v}$ on the cone is an SOS, but some $B_{p,u,v}$ is not a matrix SOS. The obstruction persists at nearby interior directions, giving a rational hyperbolicity direction at which the polynomial is weakly SOS-hyperbolic but not SOS-hyperbolic in Saunderson's fixed-direction sense. The construction is supported by exact rational Gram and trace certificates.

items.title: Approximation and Error Bounds for Zero-Sum Stopping Games with Probability Criteria
items.summary: This paper studies a two-person zero-sum stochastic game, which must terminate when either player quits the game or a state of the game first enters a prescribed target set. The performance criterion is the probability that the total reward reaches a given threshold. First, under a mild condition, we prove the existence of the value and a Nash equilibrium of the game by developing a comparison theorem. Second, for solving the game with infinite states, we develop a finite-state approximation method based on truncation, and derive explicit error bounds between the values of the truncated and original games. Third, using the error bounds, we design an effective algorithm, by which we can not only obtain any approximation of the value and Nash equilibria of the original game, but also provide convergence analysis of the approximation. Finally, a queueing example is used to illustrate the advantage of our condition and the effectiveness of our algorithm.

items.title: The Optimal Interface Method: A Modelling Paradigm for Two-Body Contact Problems via Optimal Control and $Γ$-convergence
items.summary: This paper is concerned with the derivation of a model governing the equilibrium configuration of two linearly elastic bodies that may come into contact with each other. The contact zone, or coincidence set, is an \emph{a priori} unknown of the model, and the equilibrium configuration is governed by variational inequalities. We introduce a new modelling paradigm in which the contact interface between the two linearly elastic bodies under consideration is now regarded as the \emph{primary variable} of an optimal control problem whose states are the unique solutions of two \emph{independent} unilateral contact problems for which this very contact interface represents the obstacle itself. As a result, the free boundary emerges as the solution of a low-dimensional optimisation problem rather than as the active set of coupled variational inequalities. We establish the existence and uniqueness of optimal controls minimising the reduced cost functional arising from the modelling paradigm introduced beforehand, and we show that the family of marginal energy functionals associated with such model $Γ$-converges to the energy functional associated with the original variational inequalities as the positive \emph{cost parameter} $β$ in the reduced cost functional tends to zero. This $Γ$-convergence argument also yields a characterisation of the coincidence set of the limit problem in terms of the optimal interfaces. We further show that, after a suitable regularisation, the reduced cost functional is Gâteaux differentiable, and that its Gâteaux derivative can be explicitly computed \emph{without solving any adjoint system}. Finally, we corroborate the $Γ$-convergence result obtained beforehand with numerical experiments on a simplified and exactly solvable configuration.

items.title: Minimum Sum-of-Radii Clustering with Strong and Weak Oracles
items.summary: In the minimum sum of radii (MSR) problem, the input is a set of $n$ points in a metric space and a parameter $k$, and the goal is to cover the points by at most $k$ balls, each centered at an input point, while minimizing the sum of their radii. We study MSR in the weak-strong oracle model of Bateni, Dharangutte, Jayaram, and Wang (COLT'24), where the metric is unknown and is accessed through two oracles. The answers of the weak oracle are given to us for free: for every pair of points, we receive a distance value that, with probability $δ$, is arbitrarily corrupted. Exact distances are available only through costly strong queries, where a strong query on a point reveals its exact distances to all previously strongly queried points, and the goal is to minimize the number of strong queries. For every constant $δ< 1/2$, we give the first polynomial-time algorithm that makes $O(k \log n \log\log n)$ strong point queries and, with high probability, returns an $O(1)$-approximation for MSR; the previously best algorithm required running time and a number of strong queries exponential in $k$. This is within an $O(\log\log n)$ factor of a lower bound that we prove: any constant-factor approximation that succeeds with high probability on every instance must make $Ω(k \log n)$ strong queries in expectation on some instance. The same $Ω(k \log n)$ lower bound holds for $k$-center, where it matches the known upper bound up to an $O(\log\log n)$ factor. An optimal MSR cluster can be small both in size and in radius, so a uniform sample of strongly queried points may miss it entirely. Instead, our algorithm uses a packing LP over the balls certified so far to decide which points to query next. The analysis holds against an adversary who knows which pairs are corrupted.

items.title: On Covariance Steering with Nonlinear Measurements
items.summary: This paper examines two ways nonlinear measurements complicate the statistical predictions during covariance steering. The covariance steering problem optimizes a control policy across a distribution of possible trajectories rather than a single specific trajectory. This approach has attracted growing interest as a way to account for uncertainty in aerospace applications such as trajectory optimization, stationkeeping, and landing. In many of these applications, covariance steering can account for measurement uncertainty through output feedback. Because standard formulations assume linear dynamics and measurements, applications with nonlinear measurements typically use an extended Kalman filter to estimate the state. This paper shows that techniques used to improve filter convergence, such as measurement underweighting, can reduce the accuracy of conventional covariance steering predictions by violating a key assumption. This is addressed with a new convex formulation that relaxes the assumption. This paper also demonstrates that adjusting the control policy during execution can improve agreement between predicted and actual state statistics. A numerical example of angles-only spacecraft rendezvous illustrates the benefits of the proposed method, and discussions are made regarding the implications of this generalized covariance steering formulation.

items.title: Spectral Landmarks: Alignment of Landmark Kernel Translates with the Leading Eigenfunctions of a Kernel Operator
items.summary: We study the problem of choosing $m$ landmark points so that the span of the kernel translates is as close as possible to the leading $s$-dimensional eigenspace of a positive-definite kernel. The natural measure is the Hilbert-Schmidt operator discrepancy between the reproducing-kernel-Hilbert-space (RKHS) projectors onto the two subspaces. We give a closed form spectral alignment function in terms of the truncated Mercer kernel and relate it to the classical integrated power function (Nyström trace error) through a two-sided sandwich bound. Minimizing the function by gradient descent on the landmark coordinates produces landmark sets that are evenly spaced. Theoretical results show that optimal configurations are those whose eigenfunction sampling matrix is a scaled isometry. On homogeneous spaces these are exactly the minimal equal-weight cubature rules for products of leading eigenfunctions, and for every $m\ge s$ they are the configurations whose sampled eigenfunctions form a unit-norm tight frame. Experiments on $\mathbb{S}^1$ and $\mathbb{S}^2$ agree with the theory. On the circle, with $s\le2m$ and a moderate bandwidth, every random start converges to equispaced landmarks, and on the sphere the optimizer recovers the regular tetrahedron, octahedron, and icosahedron from random starts. Finally, we analyze the numerical conditioning of the problem.
